items.followUp: How would you prepare 500 mL of 1 M NaOH solution?

rubric.why: A 1 M solution contains one mole of NaOH per litre of solution; one mole of NaOH has a mass of 40 g.
rubric.description: States the required amount of NaOH for 1 L of 1 M solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying 40 g of NaOH for a final solution volume of 1 L.

rubric.why: The solute is dissolved and the solution is made up to the required final volume.
rubric.description: Describes dissolving the NaOH and making the solution up to 1 L.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the preparation to the stated final volume.

modelAnswer: Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol⁻¹.
Weigh 40 g of NaOH and dissolve it in a small amount of distilled water.
Transfer the solution to a 1 L volumetric flask and add distilled water up to the 1 L mark.
Mix the solution thoroughly.

items.followUp: Differentiate between an oxidizing agent and a reducing agent.

rubric.why: Oxidation involves the loss of electrons.
rubric.description: Defines oxidation as loss of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that oxidation is loss of electrons.

rubric.why: Reduction involves the gain of electrons.
rubric.description: Defines reduction as gain of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that reduction is gain of electrons.

modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule.
Reduction is the gain of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule.

items.followUp: What is corrosion? State the conditions required for iron to corrode.

rubric.why: Rust is the reddish-brown iron oxide that forms on iron.
rubric.description: Defines rusting as the formation of a reddish-brown iron oxide coating on iron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition of rusting.

rubric.why: Both oxygen and moisture are required for rusting under ordinary conditions.
rubric.description: States that both oxygen and moisture are required.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both conditions.

modelAnswer: Rusting is the slow formation of a reddish-brown coating of hydrated iron(III) oxide on iron.
The important condition for rusting is the presence of both oxygen and moisture.

items.followUp: Why do metals form positive ions in chemical reactions?

rubric.why: Metals characteristically lose electrons and form positively charged ions.
rubric.description: Defines metals by their tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for stating both the loss of electrons and formation of positive ions.

modelAnswer: Metals are elements that readily lose electrons to form positively charged ions (cations).

items.followUp: Write two chemical reactions that show properties of metals.

rubric.why: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic.
rubric.description: States that metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property, with or without an example.

rubric.why: Many metals react with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas.
rubric.description: States that metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property, with or without an example.

modelAnswer: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides; for example, 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
Many metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas; for example, Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.

items.followUp: What are noble gases? Give two examples.

rubric.why: Halogens are the salt-forming elements in Group 17 of the periodic table.
rubric.description: Identifies halogens as the salt-forming elements of Group 17.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the group or their salt-forming nature.

rubric.why: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are examples of halogens.
rubric.description: Gives two correct examples of halogens.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two correct examples.

modelAnswer: Halogens are the salt-forming elements of Group 17 of the periodic table.
Examples include fluorine (F) and chlorine (Cl).

items.followUp: State Bohr's postulates about electron shells and the emission or absorption of energy.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy fixed paths or shells with definite energies.
rubric.description: States that electrons move in fixed orbits or shells with definite energies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixed-orbit or energy-level postulate.

rubric.why: Electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not radiate energy while in a stationary orbit.

rubric.why: An electron absorbs energy when it moves to a higher energy level.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher energy level.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing absorption during an upward transition.

rubric.why: An electron emits energy when it moves to a lower energy level.
rubric.description: States that an electron emits energy when it moves to a lower energy level.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing emission during a downward transition.

rubric.why: The energy emitted or absorbed equals the difference between the two energy levels and is related to radiation frequency by ΔE = hν.
rubric.description: Relates the energy change to the frequency of the emitted or absorbed radiation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the relation ΔE = hν or its equivalent statement.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain fixed circular paths called orbits or shells; each has a definite energy.
An electron in a permitted stationary orbit does not radiate or lose energy.
An electron absorbs energy and jumps to a higher energy level when it receives the required energy.
An electron emits energy and jumps to a lower energy level when it loses energy.
The energy absorbed or emitted equals the difference between the two energy levels: ΔE = hν.

items.followUp: Define a molecule and distinguish between molecules of elements and molecules of compounds, giving examples.

rubric.why: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
rubric.description: Defines a molecule as the smallest independently existing particle retaining the substance's chemical properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a substantially correct definition.

rubric.why: A molecule of an element contains atoms of the same element, such as O₂, N₂ or H₂.
rubric.description: Names molecules of elements and gives a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the type and an example.

rubric.why: A molecule of a compound contains atoms of different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, such as H₂O or CO₂.
rubric.description: Names molecules of compounds and gives a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the type and its constituent atoms; award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain the chemical properties of that substance.
Molecules of elements contain atoms of the same element; for example, O₂.
Molecules of compounds contain atoms of different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; for example, H₂O.
